title: SLI, SLO and SLA
description: Learn about SLI, SLO and SLA. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: **SLI, SLO and SLA** are the backbone of production reliability. This lesson teaches you how to define, measure, and operate these contracts so your team can ship features with confidence instead of fear.
What Are SLI, SLO, and SLA

A **Service Level Indicator (SLI)** is a carefully defined quantitative measure of service behavior. Think of it as the raw signal you collect: request latency, error rate, throughput, or freshness. An **Service Level Objective (SLO)** is the target you set for that indicator over a rolling window, such as 99.9 percent of requests returning under 200 milliseconds over 30 days. A **Service Level Agreement (SLA)** is the external or internal contract that carries consequences when the SLO is missed, often including credits, refunds, or escalation paths.

terms.definition: A quantitative measure of service behavior such as latency, error rate, throughput, or availability.
A target value for an SLI over a specified measurement window, such as 99.9 percent availability over 30 days.
A formal contract with business consequences when SLOs are missed, including credits or remediation.
The allowable difference between 100 percent and the SLO target; the budget you can spend on riskier changes.
The rate at which an error budget is being consumed, used to detect SLO risk early.

data.title: Senior Engineer Mindset
data.text: SLIs are measurement problems. SLOs are policy problems. SLAs are business problems. Separate them so you do not accidentally turn an engineering metric into a legal obligation without executive buy-in.
The Four Golden Signals

Google SRE introduced four signals that cover most user-facing services. **Latency** measures how long operations take, separating successful requests from failed ones because retries inflate average latency. **Traffic** is a measure of demand, usually requests per second, concurrent users, or bytes transferred. **Errors** is the rate of failed requests, including HTTP 500s, dropped connections, and authorization failures. **Saturation** captures how close a service is to its capacity limit, usually expressed as CPU, memory, or queue depth with headroom factored in.

items: Latency: time per request with success/failure separated
Traffic: requests per second or concurrent users
Errors: failed request rate including HTTP 5xx and dropped connections
Saturation: utilization relative to a safe capacity limit

data.text: Choosing Good SLIs

A good SLI maps directly to user experience. For a checkout service, the p99 latency of payment API calls is more meaningful than the average CPU usage. For a storage API, the proportion of requests served from cache with freshness under five minutes is more meaningful than total storage bytes. SLIs should be computable from existing telemetry, auditable by product managers, and actionable by on-call engineers.

items: Tie the SLI to a user outcome, not an internal metric
Prefer ratios over absolute counts to avoid scale dependency
Exclude planned maintenance windows if they are not user-impacting
Document the exact algorithm so it survives team turnover

data.title: Pitfall: Vanity SLIs
data.text: Avoid SLIs that are trivially easy to meet or that no one can observe. CPU utilization below 20 percent is not useful if users experience 10-second page loads. Always validate that improving the SLI improves user experience.
Setting SLOs with Discipline

SLOs should be ambitious yet achievable. A common pattern is to start from historical performance, add a margin, and then review quarterly. If your service has been 99.95 percent available over the past six months, an initial SLO of 99.9 percent gives you room to grow while protecting users. If you set the bar at 99.999 percent without the operational machinery to support it, you will burn the team out chasing impossible targets.

items: Compute the rolling 30-day and 90-day historical availability, latency, and error rates.
Identify the current pain points: which signals are closest to breaching a user's trust?
Set the first SLO one to two nines above the current failure rate.
Document the measurement window, aggregation method, and alerting threshold.
Publish the draft to stakeholders and iterate before making it contractual.

data.text: SLOs Versus SLAs

Not every SLO should become an SLA. An SLO is an internal target that drives prioritization and error budget policy. An SLA is an external contract with financial or reputational consequences. Most services have multiple SLOs but only one or two SLAs. The SLO for p99 latency might be 200 milliseconds, while the SLA might promise 99 percent of requests under one second with refunds for violations.

cards.title: SLO
cards.description: Internal target for an SLI. Drives engineering decisions and alerts. Typically tight, reviewed quarterly, and enforced through error budgets.

cards.title: SLA
cards.description: External or contractual promise to users or customers. Carries financial penalties, refunds, or support credits when breached. Wider than the SLO to provide a safety buffer.

data.text: Multi-Window, Multi-Burn-Rate Alerting

Single-window alerts fire late or too often. The multi-window, multi-burn-rate approach uses a fast window to detect sudden budget loss and a slow window to confirm chronic drift. If the burn rate in the last hour is 14.4 times the sustained budget, the fast window fires immediately. If the 24-hour burn rate exceeds six times, the medium window fires. The slow seven-day window catches gradual degradation before it hits the monthly budget.

rows: Catch sudden outages or runaway releases

data.text: Rolling Versus Calendar Windows

Rolling windows measure the last 30 days from today. Calendar windows measure a fixed month from the first to the last day. Rolling windows are smoother and easier to explain but can mask events that straddle month boundaries. Calendar windows align with finance and reporting but can surprise engineers with sudden resets at midnight on the first. Most mature SRE teams use rolling windows for operational decision-making and calendar windows for SLA reporting.

data.title: Gotcha: Window Shifting
data.text: If you alert on a rolling 30-day window, a single incident on day one can influence alerts for 30 days. Pair rolling alerts with calendar-based SLA reporting so finance and engineering speak the same language.
SLI Aggregation Methods

Raw measurements must be aggregated before they become SLIs. The choice of aggregation method changes the behavior of the indicator. **Mean** is easy to compute but hides outliers. **Median** is robust to outliers but can still hide long tails. **p99** captures the worst experience for the slowest 1 percent of users. **Ratio** counts good events over total events, which normalizes traffic changes.

items: Mean: simple average; useful for CPU or memory saturation
Median: 50th percentile; robust but hides tail latency
p90, p95, p99: tail latency; critical for user-facing latency SLIs
Ratio: good events divided by total events; preferred for availability and error-rate SLIs
Percentile difference: p99 minus p50; indicates tail bloat

data.text: The User Journey SLI

End-to-end latency across a multi-service request path can be more important than any single service's latency. A checkout flow might touch the product catalog, cart, identity, payment, and order services. If the payment service is fast but the cart service is slow, the user still waits. Measuring the entire journey gives the on-call engineer the right signal to debug user pain.

data.title: E-commerce Checkout Journey
data.content: The checkout SLI measures the time from the user clicking Place Order to the confirmation page rendering. The SLO requires 95 percent of checkouts to complete within 3 seconds. The team instruments the journey by emitting a start event at the API gateway and an end event in the confirmation page, then aggregates the latency in a time-series database.
data.code:
# Pseudocode for journey latency SLI
start_events = gateway.filter(event='order_start')
end_events = confirmation.filter(event='order_complete')
latencies = join(start_events, end_events, key=request_id)
checkout_p95 = latencies.quantile(0.95)

slo_check = checkout_p95 <= 3000ms
budget_remaining = 1 - (violation_rate / (1 - 0.99))

data.text: Alerting on SLI Budgets

Alerting on absolute latency thresholds produces brittle alerts. Alerting on error budget consumption is more robust because it scales with the SLO. A five nines service can tolerate 26 minutes of downtime per month. A four nines service can tolerate 4.3 hours. The same number of errors consumes very different fractions of budget depending on the SLO. Always alert on budget burn rate, not raw error count.

items: Define the monthly error budget from the SLO: budget equals the difference between 100 percent and the target.
Instrument each good and bad event into the SLI calculation.
Compute rolling burn rate as consumed budget divided by elapsed time of the window.
Fire fast alerts when the burn rate exceeds the multiplier in the alerting policy.
Tie every alert to a runbook so the on-call engineer knows the remediation steps.

data.text: Reviewing SLO Performance

SLOs should be reviewed in a structured SLO review meeting every four to eight weeks. The review covers the current error budget status, the biggest contributors to budget burn, upcoming changes that might accelerate burn, and whether the SLO is still aligned with user expectations. Product managers, SREs, and engineering managers should attend. The output is either a renewed commitment to the current SLO, a proposal to raise or lower it, or a decision to invest in reliability to protect the budget.

items.item: Report current error budget status and burn rate trend
Rank the top three contributors to budget consumption
Review upcoming deploys, migrations, and marketing campaigns
Discuss user complaints and support tickets related to reliability
Propose adjustments to the SLO or SLI definition
Assign owners for reliability improvement work items

data.text: SLA Design for Customer Contracts

When designing an SLA for external customers, add a safety cushion below the SLO so that minor SLO misses do not immediately breach the contract. A common pattern is a 99.9 percent SLO with a 99.5 percent SLA, giving a four nines service a tenfold buffer before credits are owed. Define service credits as a percentage of the monthly invoice, specify the claim process, and cap liability at the amount paid in the preceding billing cycle.

data.title: Sample SLA Terms
data.content: Monthly Uptime SLA: 99.9 percent. If monthly uptime falls between 99.0 percent and 99.9 percent, the customer receives a 10 percent credit on the next invoice. If uptime falls between 98.0 percent and 99.0 percent, the customer receives a 25 percent credit. Below 98.0 percent, the customer receives a 50 percent credit. Credits must be claimed within 30 days of the billing cycle.

data.text: SLOs for Internal APIs

Internal services benefit from SLOs even without external SLAs. A payment service might define an SLO of 99.95 percent successful transactions over 30 days and 50 milliseconds p50 latency. The inventory service might define an SLO of 99 percent cache hit rate with freshness under five minutes. Each team writes and owns its SLOs, but a platform SRE team can audit them for consistency and support the measurement infrastructure.

items: Payment service: 99.95 percent success, 50 ms p50 latency
Inventory service: 99 percent cache hit rate, 5-minute freshness
Notification service: 99 percent delivery within 5 seconds
Search service: 95 percent of queries under 200 ms
Auth service: 99.99 percent successful token refresh

data.text: SLO Burnout and Recovery

When a service misses its SLO, the error budget is exhausted. The correct response is a freeze on risky changes, not an all-hands firefight. The team should assess the blast radius, identify the root cause, and prioritize fixes that restore the budget. If the budget is exhausted mid-month, consider a feature freeze on that service while allowing safe dependency patches and security updates. Do not approve new experiments or launches until the burn rate drops below one times.

data.title: SLO Exhaustion Playbook
data.text: Stop risky launches, hold a war room to identify the largest budget consumers, assign owners to reliability work, communicate status to product stakeholders, and only lift the freeze when the 24-hour burn rate drops below 1.0.
Freeze Thresholds and Change Gates

Automated change gates block high-risk deployments when the error budget is low. A typical gate triggers at 10 percent remaining budget and blocks all non-critical launches. At 0 percent remaining, the gate blocks all code pushes to the service. The gate should have an emergency override process that requires sign-off from two on-call engineers and a 24-hour cool-down before the override expires.

items: At 10 percent budget remaining: alert the team, increase code review scrutiny, and warn product.
At 0 percent budget remaining: freeze risky launches, require director sign-off for non-critical changes.
At 0 percent with user impact: escalate to senior leadership, consider page-wide rollback.
Emergency override: requires two on-call sign-offs, logs the decision, and expires in 24 hours.

data.text: SLOs and Organizational Culture

SLOs only work if the organization respects the error budget. If leadership punishes every outage regardless of budget status, engineers will hide incidents and under-report errors. The SLO becomes a political tool rather than a reliability tool. Successful SLO cultures treat budget expenditure as a normal cost of innovation. When the budget is healthy, teams ship faster. When the budget is low, teams slow down and invest in reliability.
SLOs are not about being perfect. They are about being honest and predictable.
SLI Implementation in Prometheus

Prometheus SLI definitions are PromQL queries that compute a ratio over a time window. An availability SLI counts successful HTTP requests divided by total requests. A latency SLI counts requests under the threshold divided by total requests. Both must filter out non-service traffic such as health checks, metrics scraping, and canary probes to avoid distorting the ratio.

data.title: Prometheus SLI Queries
data.content: The following queries define availability and latency SLIs for an HTTP service. The availability SLI excludes health-check traffic. The latency SLI counts requests under 200 ms as good.
data.code:
# Availability SLI: successful requests / total requests
availability_sli = sum(rate(http_requests_total{status!~"5..", job="api"}[30d])) /
                 sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[30d]))

# Latency SLI: requests under 200ms / total requests
latency_sli = sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.2", job="api"}[30d])) /
              sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="api"}[30d]))

data.text: SLOs with Bigtable and Monarch

Large organizations use systems such as Google Monarch, Prometheus with Thanos, or commercial APM tools to store SLI data at scale. Monarch stores time-series data in Bigtable and computes SLOs across thousands of services. The architecture supports rollups at multiple granularities, from one-second raw samples to daily summaries. When designing SLIs for Monarch, ensure the underlying metric has a cardinality limit that prevents runaway storage costs.

data.title: Cardinality Hygiene
data.text: Avoid high-cardinality labels on SLI metrics. A label like user_id can explode into billions of series. Use aggregation or sampling for user-level SLIs and reserve high cardinality for debugging, not SLO computation.
SLOs for Mobile and Client-Side Applications

Mobile applications introduce SLI challenges that server-side metrics do not capture. Users on spotty networks experience launch timeouts and failed syncs. Device fragmentation means p99 latency on a flagship phone is not the same as p99 latency on a budget Android device. Client-side telemetry platforms such as Firebase Performance Monitoring or Datadog RUM emit SLIs from real user devices, giving a signal that mirrors actual user pain.

items: App startup time: time from icon tap to interactive UI
Network request success: successful API calls divided by total attempts
Crash-free rate: sessions without a crash divided by total sessions
API latency: round-trip time for critical endpoints from real devices

data.text: Latency Percentiles in Depth

Mean latency is almost always the wrong SLI for user-facing services. A service with mean latency of 100 ms and p99 of 2 seconds looks healthy on dashboards, but the slowest 1 percent of users are miserable. Always choose a tail percentile that maps to the user experience. For APIs, p95 and p99 are standard. For real-time applications such as gaming or video, p50 might be the right choice because even small jitter is noticeable.

rows: Resolver fan-out makes p99 too noisy
Jitter sensitivity makes median more relevant
Users tolerate more variance for background work

data.text: Availability SLIs for Microservices

A microservice should define availability at its own boundary, not at the API gateway. If the product service is healthy but the recommendation service is down, the product service is still available even though the full page experience is degraded. Defining SLIs per service allows owners to focus on their blast radius while a platform team defines page-level SLIs for overall user experience.

items: Service-level SLI: 200 OK responses divided by total requests to that service.
Dependency-level SLI: successful downstream calls divided by total calls.
Page-level SLI: end-to-end successful page loads divided by total page loads.
Business SLI: successful checkout flows divided by initiated checkouts.

data.text: Error Rate SLIs

Error rate SLIs count the proportion of requests that result in a user-visible failure. HTTP 500 and 502 errors are clear signals. HTTP 429 rate-limit responses are borderline: they prevent worse failures but still impact the user. HTTP 4xx client errors are usually excluded because they represent misuse rather than service failure. The SLI definition should explicitly list which status codes count as errors.

items: Count 500, 502, 503, 504 as errors
Exclude 400 and 401 unless they indicate a service bug
Include 429 if it blocks user progress
Exclude health checks and internal probes
Count GRPC UNAVAILABLE and DEADLINE_EXCEEDED as errors

data.text: Freshness SLIs for Data Pipelines

Data pipelines need SLIs that measure staleness, not just throughput. A pipeline that processes one billion events per day but is six hours behind is not useful for real-time dashboards. A freshness SLI measures the proportion of events processed within a target window, such as 95 percent of events appearing in the dashboard within 10 minutes of ingestion.

data.title: Pipeline Freshness SLI
data.content: The data freshness SLI counts events whose processing timestamp is within 10 minutes of their ingestion timestamp, divided by total events ingested in the window.
data.code:
# Freshness SLI for a Kafka-to-Bigtable pipeline
freshness_sli = sum(rate(events_processed_lag_seconds_bucket{le=600}[30d])) /
                sum(rate(events_processed_total[30d]))

# The le=600 bucket counts events processed within 600 seconds of ingestion.

data.text: Throughput SLIs

Throughput SLIs measure whether a system can handle its expected load. Instead of measuring requests per second directly, define the SLI as the proportion of time the system operates above a minimum throughput threshold. For example, 99 percent of minutes should process at least 1000 requests per second. This avoids alerting during predictable off-peak hours while still catching capacity regressions.

items: Minimum throughput: 1000 RPS 99 percent of the time
Peak capacity: sustain 5000 RPS without saturation
Queue depth: P99 queue length under 100 messages
Connection pool: utilization below 80 percent

data.text: Saturation SLIs

Saturation SLIs measure how close a resource is to its hard limit. CPU saturation above 80 percent for sustained periods usually predicts queue buildup and latency spikes. Memory saturation above 90 percent triggers OOM kills. Disk saturation above 85 percent degrades write latency. Define saturation SLIs with a safety margin so you have headroom to absorb traffic spikes before the hard limit is hit.
Composite SLIs

Some services need composite SLIs that combine multiple signals. A good composite SLI weights each signal by user impact. A checkout service might weight availability at 40 percent, latency at 40 percent, and correctness at 20 percent. When the composite SLI breaches the SLO, the team knows the service is failing across multiple dimensions simultaneously.

data.title: Composite SLI Formula
data.content: The composite SLI for checkout is the weighted sum of availability, latency, and correctness SLIs. If any single component drops below 95 percent of its SLO, the composite is considered at risk.
data.code:
composite_sli = (
  0.40 * availability_sli +
  0.40 * latency_sli +
  0.20 * correctness_sli
)

at_risk = (
  availability_sli < 0.95 * availability_slo or
  latency_sli < 0.95 * latency_slo or
  correctness_sli < 0.95 * correctness_slo
)

data.text: SLI Measurement Windows

The measurement window determines how responsive the SLI is to change. A one-minute window is too noisy for strategic decisions but excellent for real-time alerting. A 30-day window is ideal for SLO tracking but too slow to detect acute incidents. Most mature systems use multiple windows simultaneously: a one-minute window for page-level alerts, a one-hour window for SRE triage, and a 30-day window for error budget and SLO review.

items: 1-minute window: page on-call for acute incidents
1-hour window: SRE triage and immediate response
24-hour window: daily standup review
30-day rolling window: error budget and SLO tracking
Calendar month: SLA reporting and finance

data.text: SLI Exclusion Criteria

Not all traffic should count toward the SLI. Health checks, load balancer probes, synthetic monitoring, and internal service-to-service traffic can distort the ratio. Define exclusion criteria explicitly in the SLI documentation. For example, exclude requests with the header X-Health-Check or requests from the monitoring namespace. Review exclusions quarterly to ensure they are not hiding real problems.

data.title: Exclusion Drift
data.text: If exclusions grow beyond 20 percent of traffic, the SLI no longer reflects real user experience. Investigate why so much traffic is being excluded and whether the exclusion criteria need tightening.
SLO-Driven Change Management

SLOs change how teams prioritize work. When the error budget is healthy, the team can accept more risk and ship faster. When the budget is burning fast, the team must slow down and invest in reliability. This creates a natural feedback loop without requiring top-down edicts. Engineering managers can reference the error budget in planning meetings: do we have enough budget to take on this feature?

items: At the start of each quarter, review the current error budget and project the burn rate for planned work.
If the projected burn exceeds the budget, prioritize reliability work over features.
If the budget is healthy, approve riskier experiments and feature launches.
Mid-quarter, reassess after each incident. If an incident consumed a large fraction of budget, rebalance the roadmap.
End-of-quarter, present the SLO review to leadership with concrete evidence of stability or instability.

data.text: SLI and SLO Documentation Standards

Every SLO should live in a shared runbook or wiki page that includes the SLI definition, the measurement algorithm, the current value, the target value, the measurement window, the alerting policy, the escalation path, and the last review date. When the definition changes, the runbook must be updated before the new definition goes live. This ensures the on-call engineer always knows what the alert means.

items.item: SLI formula and source metric defined
SLO target value and measurement window documented
Alerting policy with burn-rate thresholds listed
Runbook link attached to every alert
Escalation path and on-call owner identified
Last review date and next review date recorded

data.text: SLA Penalty Structures

Penalty structures should be proportional, predictable, and easy to claim. A tiered credit structure is standard: 10 percent for minor misses, 25 percent for moderate, and 50 percent for severe. Define the exact uptime percentage for each tier, set a maximum credit equal to one or two months of fees, and require customers to submit claims within 30 days. Automate credit calculation where possible to reduce disputes.
Negotiating SLAs with Customers

Customers often demand 99.99 percent SLAs without understanding the cost. As a senior engineer, translate availability numbers into concrete terms: 99.99 percent allows 52 minutes of downtime per year, roughly one four-hour incident per quarter. Explain the operational cost of that target and propose alternatives such as a 99.9 percent SLA with a financial penalty or a 99.99 percent SLA at a higher price tier with dedicated on-call coverage.

items: Convert availability nines to downtime hours for stakeholder comprehension
Propose tiered SLAs so customers can self-select based on budget
Document exclusions for planned maintenance and force majeure
Include an SLA review clause every six or twelve months

data.text: SLO Budget Replenishment

Error budgets replenish on the measurement window schedule. A 30-day rolling budget replenishes continuously: as each day passes, the previous day's errors age out. A calendar-month budget replenishes all at once on the first of the month. Rolling budgets are easier to operate because they do not have cliff-edge resets. Calendar budgets are easier to communicate to finance. Use rolling for operations and calendar for reporting.

data.title: Budget Math
data.text: For a 99.9 percent monthly SLO, the error budget is 43.2 minutes of downtime per 30-day month. If a two-hour incident consumes the entire budget, the team must freeze risky changes until enough time passes for the rolling window to shed the incident.
SLO Monitoring Dashboards

Every SLO needs a dashboard that shows the current SLI value, the SLO target, the remaining error budget, the burn rate over multiple windows, and the top contributors to budget consumption. Grafana dashboards with SLO-specific panels are standard. Include a timeline view so engineers can correlate budget spikes with deploys or incidents.

items: Current SLI value and target displayed prominently
Error budget remaining as a percentage and a time equivalent
Burn rate sparklines for 1-hour, 6-hour, 24-hour, and 7-day windows
Top contributors table sorted by budget consumption
Deploy markers overlaid on the timeline
Incident markers with duration and impact

data.text: Automated SLO Reporting

Automated weekly or monthly SLO reports reduce manual toil. The report should summarize SLI performance, budget consumption, incident contributions, and upcoming risk factors. Distribute it to engineering leadership, product managers, and customer success teams. Automate the report with Grafana, Datadog, or a custom Slack bot that posts a summary every Monday morning.

data.title: Weekly SLO Report Format
data.content: The automated report covers the current SLI value, remaining budget, burn rate trend, top contributors, and a risk forecast. Format it as a Slack message or email digest.
data.code:
SLI: checkout availability = 99.94 percent (SLO 99.9 percent)
Budget: 6 percent remaining (2.6 days at current burn)
Burn: 1.2x sustained, 3.4x last 24 hours
Top contributors:
  1. Payment gateway timeouts (40 percent of budget)
  2. Redis connection pool exhaustion (25 percent)
  3. Deployment latency spikes (15 percent)
Risk: Black Friday traffic spike in 3 days. Recommend freezing risky changes.

data.text: SLOs in the SDLC

SLOs should influence every stage of the software development lifecycle. During design, architects should estimate how a new feature affects error budgets. During implementation, developers should add instrumentation for the relevant SLIs. During code review, reviewers should check for SLI regressions. During launch, product managers should confirm the error budget can absorb the added risk. After launch, the team should monitor the SLI for 48 hours before declaring success.

items: Design: estimate SLI impact of new features
Implementation: instrument SLIs before shipping
Code review: check for SLI regressions
Launch: confirm error budget has headroom
Post-launch: monitor SLI for 48 hours

data.text: SLO Budget Trades with Feature Velocity

Every organization must decide how much reliability to buy with feature velocity. A startup might accept 99 percent availability and ship daily to win market share. An enterprise payment processor might demand 99.99 percent and ship weekly. Neither choice is universally correct. SLOs make the trade-off explicit so the conversation happens in planning meetings rather than after a public outage.
If you are not measuring it, you cannot manage it. If you are managing it without a target, you are guessing.
Multi-Tenant SLOs

SaaS platforms often serve customers with different SLO requirements. Enterprise customers on premium tiers might demand 99.99 percent availability while startup customers on basic tiers accept 99 percent. Multi-tenant SLOs should be enforced at the tenant boundary using rate limiting, priority queues, or dedicated infrastructure for premium tiers. Define the SLOs in the customer contract and instrument per-tenant SLIs to verify compliance.

items: Basic tier: 99 percent monthly availability
Business tier: 99.9 percent monthly availability
Enterprise tier: 99.99 percent monthly availability
Enforce with per-tenant SLI queries and alerting
Route premium traffic to dedicated capacity pools

data.text: SLI and SLO for Serverless Functions

Serverless platforms abstract infrastructure away but still need SLIs. Cold start latency is the most important SLI for serverless APIs. Define it as the proportion of invocations with latency under 200 milliseconds, excluding errors. The SLO should account for the cold start distribution: a small fraction of cold starts is acceptable, but sustained high cold start rates indicate a capacity or memory-configuration problem.

data.title: Serverless Cold Start SLI
data.content: Measure cold start latency by tagging invocations that required initialization. Compute the SLI as the ratio of warm invocations under 200 ms plus cold invocations under 500 ms, divided by total invocations.
data.code:
# CloudWatch metric math for cold start SLI
cold_start_sli = (
  SUM(METRICS()["Duration", "FunctionName", "cold", {stat: "Sum", unit: "Milliseconds"}]) +
  SUM(METRICS()["Duration", "FunctionName", "warm", {stat: "Sum", unit: "Milliseconds", filter: "lt:200"}])
) / SUM(METRICS()["Invocations", "FunctionName", {}])

data.text: SLI and SLO for Message Queues

Message queue systems need SLIs that measure delivery latency, throughput, and data loss. A queue SLI might measure the proportion of messages delivered within 100 milliseconds of publish. An SLO might require 99.9 percent of messages delivered within one second. Data loss SLIs are binary: zero tolerance for unacknowledged message drops in financial systems, but small tolerances in analytics pipelines.

items: Publish-to-deliver latency: 99 percent under 100 ms
Delivery success rate: 99.99 percent of published messages delivered
Queue depth: 95 percent under 10,000 messages
Consumer lag: 99 percent under 5 seconds behind producer

data.text: SLI and SLO for Databases

Database SLIs should measure query latency, connection pool utilization, replication lag, and error rate. A relational database SLO might require p99 query latency under 100 milliseconds and replication lag under one second. A NoSQL database SLO might measure p99 read latency under 50 milliseconds and write latency under 100 milliseconds. Always include a data-loss SLI with zero tolerance for OLTP systems.
SLO Alert Design Patterns

Good SLO alerts are specific, actionable, and proportional. A vague alert saying service is degraded is useless to an on-call engineer. An alert that says checkout availability SLI is at 40 percent remaining budget with a 14.4x burn rate due to payment gateway timeouts tells the engineer exactly what to investigate and which runbook to follow.

items: Alert name includes the service, SLI, and window: checkout-availability-1h
Alert description includes the current SLI, remaining budget, and burn rate
Runbook link is the first thing in the alert message
Severity matches burn-rate multiplier: warning at 3x, critical at 14.4x
Include the top contributor as a dimension in the alert payload

data.text: SLO Burn Rate Math

Understanding burn rate math is essential for SREs. If the monthly SLO is 99.9 percent, the error budget is 0.1 percent. A 14.4x burn rate means the service is consuming error budget 14.4 times faster than the sustainable rate. At that rate, the entire monthly budget is exhausted in approximately 30 days divided by 14.4, or roughly two days. The fast window alerts immediately so the team can stop the bleeding.

data.title: Burn Rate Calculation
data.content: Calculate the time to exhaust the error budget at a given burn rate. A 14.4x burn rate on a 30-day budget exhausts it in roughly 2 days.
data.code:
slo = 0.999
monthly_budget_days = 30
budget = 1 - slo

# If error rate is 14.4x the sustainable rate
error_rate = (1 - slo) * 14.4
time_to_exhaust = monthly_budget_days / 14.4
print(f"Time to exhaust budget: {time_to_exhaust:.1f} days")
# Output: Time to exhaust budget: 2.1 days

data.text: SLO Review Meeting Template

The SLO review meeting should follow a consistent template to maximize efficiency. Open with the current error budget chart. Discuss incidents from the review period and their budget impact. Review upcoming launches and assess the projected burn. Close with action items and owners. The meeting should take no more than 30 minutes for a small service and 60 minutes for a large service.

items.item: Open with current error budget dashboard (5 minutes)
Review incidents and budget impact from the period (10 minutes)
Assess upcoming launches and projected burn (10 minutes)
Propose SLO adjustments if needed (5 minutes)
Assign action items and set deadlines (5 minutes)

data.text: Cross-Functional SLO Ownership

SLOs require collaboration between engineering, product, and customer success. Engineering owns the instrumentation and infrastructure. Product owns the SLO target and the trade-off with features. Customer success translates the SLO into customer-facing language. Document the owners for each SLO in a shared registry. When an SLO is breached, the notification should go to all three functions.

items: Engineering: instrumentation, alerting, and runbooks
Product: target selection, budget allocation, and release decisions
Customer success: contract translation and customer communication
All three: SLO review attendance and incident response

data.text: SLOs and Postmortems

Every postmortem for an SLO-missed incident should quantify the budget impact. How many minutes or hours of budget did the incident consume? What fraction of the monthly budget is that? If the incident consumed more than 25 percent of the budget, the action items should include a dedicated reliability sprint. This quantification turns vague lessons into concrete prioritization inputs for the next planning cycle.

data.title: Budget Quantification
data.text: Always include the exact error budget consumption in postmortems. A two-hour outage on a 99.9 percent service consumes approximately 28 percent of the monthly budget. That number is more persuasive than any qualitative description.
SLOs for Batch and ETL Systems

Batch systems do not serve requests in real time, so traditional latency SLIs do not apply. Instead, define SLIs based on job completion time, data freshness, and success rate. A daily ETL pipeline might define an SLO of 99 percent of runs completing within 30 minutes of the scheduled start time. A streaming pipeline might define an SLO of 99 percent of events processed within five minutes of ingestion.

items: Job completion: 99 percent finish within 30 minutes of schedule
Data freshness: 99 percent of events under 5 minutes old
Success rate: 99.5 percent of daily runs succeed on first attempt
Recovery time: 95 percent of failed jobs retry and succeed within 1 hour

data.text: SLOs and Chaos Engineering

Chaos engineering validates that your SLOs are realistic. By injecting failures in production or staging, you learn how much error budget a typical incident consumes. If a chaos experiment that kills 10 percent of instances consumes 40 percent of the monthly budget, you know that two such incidents would exhaust the budget. This informs both the SLO target and the architectural investment needed to protect it.

items: Run chaos experiments in production with canary blast radius.
Measure the SLI impact and error budget consumption for each experiment.
If a single experiment consumes more than 10 percent of the monthly budget, escalate.
Use the data to justify architectural improvements in planning meetings.

data.text: SLOs for Third-Party Dependencies

You own the reliability your users experience, not the third-party services you call. If a payment gateway is down, your checkout service is degraded. Define SLIs at the boundary of your service and include downstream failures in the count. For example, if the payment gateway returns a 502, count that as an error in your checkout SLI even though the root cause is external.

data.title: Downstream Error Budget
data.text: Track third-party error budget separately. If 30 percent of your budget is consumed by external failures, you have only 70 percent left for your own mistakes. Use this data in vendor reviews and contract negotiations.
SLOs and Incident Response

During an incident, the error budget dashboard should be one of the first tools the incident commander opens. It tells you how much runway you have. If the burn rate is 10x and the budget is at 20 percent, you have minutes, not hours. This urgency shapes the response strategy: do you roll back, feature-flag, or fight through?

items: Open the error budget dashboard as a shared screen in the war room
Read the burn rate and remaining budget to set the urgency tone
If budget is below 10 percent, escalate to leadership immediately
If budget is above 50 percent, take a measured approach
Post the budget snapshot in the incident channel every 15 minutes

data.text: SLOs and Feature Flags

Feature flags let you decouple deployment from launch. Roll out a flag to 1 percent of users and watch the SLI. If the SLI stays green, gradually increase to 5 percent, 25 percent, and 100 percent. If the SLI dips, kill the flag. This limits the blast radius of a bad release and preserves the error budget. Define a flag-specific error budget allocation: a new feature might consume up to 20 percent of the monthly budget.

data.title: Progressive Rollout with SLO Gates
data.content: The rollout automation checks the SLI at each stage. If the SLI drops below 99.5 percent of its SLO target, the rollout pauses automatically.
data.code:
stages = [1, 5, 25, 50, 100]
for pct in stages:
    rollout(flag="new-checkout", percentage=pct)
    sli = query_checkout_sli(window="1h")
    if sli < 0.995 * checkout_slo:
        kill_flag("new-checkout")
        alert_oncall("SLO gate triggered at " + str(pct) + "%")
        break

data.text: SLOs for Scheduled Maintenance Windows

Planned maintenance such as database migrations or infrastructure upgrades consumes error budget even though it is intentional. Define a maintenance window policy that excludes planned downtime from the SLI calculation or allocates a specific maintenance budget. For example, allow four hours of planned downtime per month that does not count toward the SLO. Communicate the schedule to stakeholders so they are not surprised.

items: Exclude maintenance windows from the SLI using time-based filters
Publish the maintenance calendar at least two weeks in advance
Allocate a maximum of 4 to 8 hours per month for planned downtime
Track unplanned downtime separately from planned downtime

data.text: SLOs and Compliance

Regulatory frameworks such as SOC 2, HIPAA, and PCI-DSS often mandate specific availability targets. SLOs can serve as evidence of compliance during audits. Export SLO dashboards and historical SLI data as PDFs or CSVs. Document the measurement methodology, the retention period for telemetry data, and the access controls on the observability platform. Keep audit trails for at least one year.

data.title: Audit Trail
data.text: Retain SLO calculation inputs for at least 12 months. Enable immutable logging on the metrics backend. Export quarterly SLO reports as PDFs and store them in the compliance repository.
SLO Onboarding for New Teams

When a new team adopts SLOs, start with one SLI and one SLO. Do not try to instrument everything at once. Choose the signal closest to the user, set a realistic target based on two weeks of historical data, and review it in two weeks. After the first SLO is stable, add a second signal such as latency or saturation. This incremental approach prevents teams from abandoning SLOs because of setup fatigue.

items: Week 1: instrument one SLI, define one SLO
Week 2: review the SLO, adjust if needed
Week 3-4: add a second SLI and SLO
Month 2: set up alerting and runbooks
Month 3: conduct the first formal SLO review

data.text: Common SLO Anti-Patterns

SLOs fail when teams game the metrics or ignore the user. Anti-patterns include setting the SLO equal to current performance with no stretch, measuring infrastructure health instead of user experience, chasing every alert without prioritization, and treating SLO misses as shame rather than learning opportunities. Recognize these anti-patterns in retrospectives and correct them.

items: Vanity SLO: target matches current performance with no stretch goal
Infrastructure SLO: measures CPU instead of user experience
Alert fatigue: too many low-priority SLO alerts desensitize the team
Blame culture: SLO misses trigger punishment instead of investment
Ignoring SLI drift: failing to update SLIs when the product changes

data.text: SLO Maturity Model

Mature SLO programs progress through five levels. Level one is ad-hoc with no formal SLIs. Level two defines a few SLIs but has no SLOs or alerting. Level three has SLOs and dashboards but no error budget policy. Level four has full error budget policies, alerts, and change gates. Level five has automated governance, predictive burn-rate modeling, and AI-assisted anomaly detection on SLI data.
SLO Governance

SLO governance ensures that targets are set responsibly, reviewed regularly, and enforced consistently across the organization. A governance board or SRE council should approve new SLOs, audit existing ones, and resolve conflicts when service SLIs overlap. The board should meet monthly and publish a registry of all active SLOs with their owners, targets, and review dates.

items: Approve new SLOs before they go live
Audit SLOs quarterly for relevance and accuracy
Resolve conflicts between service-level and page-level SLIs
Publish a central SLO registry with owners and review dates
Track SLO maturity across all teams

data.text: SLO Communication Strategies

Translating SLOs for non-technical stakeholders is a key senior engineer skill. Instead of saying our availability SLI is 99.94 percent with a burn rate of 1.2x, say we have used 60 percent of our monthly reliability budget and are on track. If an incident consumes 30 percent, say that one outage cost us almost a third of our monthly budget. Use analogies such as a bank account or a gas tank to make the budget tangible.
The best SLO is the one that product managers understand and engineers trust.
Future Directions in SLOs

The next generation of SLO tooling uses machine learning to predict error budget exhaustion before it happens. Predictive models trained on historical SLI data, deploy frequency, and incident patterns can forecast budget consumption with 80 percent accuracy one week ahead. This gives teams time to slow down before the budget is gone. Watch the SLO-cpp project, the OpenSLO specification, and vendor tooling from Grafana and Google for emerging standards.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: SLIs are measurements, SLOs are targets, and SLAs are contracts with consequences.
Use the four golden signals as a starting point for SLI selection.
Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting balances responsiveness with stability.
Error budgets enable data-driven trade-offs between feature velocity and reliability.
Document every SLO with its definition, target, window, and alerting policy.
Review SLOs regularly with cross-functional stakeholders to keep them relevant.
data.takeaway: Mastering SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs turns reliability from a cost center into a strategic advantage.

items.question: What is the difference between an SLI and an SLO?
items.answer: An SLI is a measurement such as latency or error rate. An SLO is a target for that measurement over a window, such as 99.9 percent availability over 30 days.

items.question: How many SLOs should a service have?
items.answer: Start with two to four. Add more only when the current set does not capture an important user pain point.

items.question: Should I set my SLO at current performance or higher?
items.answer: Set it one to two nines above current performance. If you are at 99.5 percent, start at 99.9 percent and ratchet up as you improve.

items.question: What happens when the error budget is exhausted?
items.answer: Freeze risky changes, prioritize reliability work, and only resume feature launches when the burn rate drops below 1.0.

items.question: Do SLAs and SLOs need to match?
items.answer: No. SLAs should have a safety cushion below the SLO so that minor SLO misses do not immediately trigger financial penalties.
